prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have moved from B034 to B042 with Katori and Ye, and I want to say why in scientific terms. My first-round reservation about the lattice clock was what new principle it adds beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems. Having read the full exchange, I think the answer is concrete and I can judge it from outside atomic physics. The magic-wavelength condition is a cancellation argument: the trap light shifts the two clock levels equally, so the trap does not perturb the transition to first order. That is what allows a very large number of neutral atoms to be held tightly in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated at once, which gives the statistical power that a single ion cannot. This is a new principle, not a better ion clock, and it is the reason the systematic uncertainty could be pushed to about 10^-18 in several species and several laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg), with comparisons between institutions. Maturity is therefore not in question. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori as originator of the concept, Ye as the person whose group drove the many-atom clock to the lowest systematic uncertainty and made inter-laboratory comparison routine. Lindroth asked whether agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage reflects shared bias. I do not have that vantage, I did not rank this candidate first, and I still find the case sound on its merits. That is a modest data point, but it is independent of the AMO members.
statement.case_against: I keep my own earlier case, KPZ universality, as an alternative, so I state what stops me from preferring it. Only I ranked it first or at all, and that alone is not an argument; the real obstacles are scientific. Parisi co-authored the 1986 paper, the exact solutions that gave the field its depth (Johansson, Prahofer-Spohn, Sasamoto-Spohn, Amir-Corwin-Quastel) lie outside a Kardar-Zhang-Takeuchi trio, and experimental universality rests mainly on liquid-crystal turbulence and a few other systems. I could not give the committee a three-name credit that I would defend without a long list of caveats. Against B042 itself the objections stand. Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde are outside the two names, and the first strontium lattice-clock demonstrations are not Katori's or Ye's alone. Ye's reputation also rests partly on comb and ultrastable-laser work already honoured in 2005. The second has not yet been redefined, and a reader can see the lattice clock as the third prize in one lineage. I think the citation must be narrow enough to avoid claiming the comb, the thorium nuclear clock or the whole of optical metrology.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a single, identifiable achievement with a clean causal chain from Katori's magic-wavelength proposal to the many-atom Lamb-Dicke architecture and to uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduced in several species and laboratories.
responses.response: I agree with this, and it is the argument that moved me. In round 1 I asked what new principle the lattice clock adds beyond 2005 and 2012. Your chain answers it: the shift cancellation turns a trap into a non-perturbing container for many atoms. I disagree with one thing. You list the pending redefinition of the second as part of the impact, and I would leave it out. The prize should rest on what has been demonstrated, as you say yourself in your uncertainties, and the citation should not wait for or depend on a metrological decision.

responses.point: A lattice clock is partly an engineering refinement of ideas honoured in 2005 and 2012, and agreement on it among members with an atomic-physics vantage should not be taken as evidence of merit.
responses.response: I take the second point seriously and I am answering it as a member from outside AMO. I do not think the engineering reading holds. The 2005 prize covered comb-based frequency measurement and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems; neither contains the idea that a lattice can be made light-shift-free for the clock transition so that thousands of atoms are interrogated together. That is where the stability gain comes from, and independent groups reproduced it. I agree with your reservation on Takamoto, Lemonde and others and I think it should shape the citation, which should name the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at 1e-18, not clocks in general.

responses.point: The Higgs observation answers a half-century question that the 2013 theory prize did not cover, and Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are a defensible trio as founding proposers and leaders; if no defensible three names exist the committee should turn elsewhere.
responses.response: I accept the correction that the 2013 prize concerned the mechanism and says nothing about the observation, and I withdraw any implication that it already covers the experiment. We agree on the last condition, and I think the chair's question shows why it applies here: no member has stated what each of the three did in the 2012 observation, and a leadership proxy for thousands of people is not something I can defend in a citation. I would not block B026, but I cannot put it ahead of a case with a clean two-person credit. I also note that you said you would not object strongly if the committee settled on Katori and Ye, which is where I have ended up.

responses.point: The citation for the lattice clock should be built around the lattice-trapping architecture and its 10^-18 performance, so that the novelty relative to the comb and ion-control prizes is explicit, and the thorium nuclear clock should stay out.
responses.response: I agree on both points and have written my citation that way: the magic-wavelength trap and the fractional uncertainty it reaches, with no mention of combs or the nuclear clock. I would add that this wording also handles the credit problem for Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde better than a generic wording, since it claims the concept and the demonstrated performance and not every step. I note your concern about a close follow-on to the 2025 circuit prize; it counts for me against B033 now, so I no longer prefer it and have not listed it as an alternative.

responses.point: Katori and Ye is a serious rival to tunnel magnetoresistance, but calling the pairing clean understates the problem that Ido, Takamoto and Lemonde are outside it, and the committee should settle whether the prize is for the concept or for record accuracy.
responses.response: That is the right question and my answer is both, stated precisely: Katori for the concept, and Ye for realising it at the lowest systematic uncertainty and making comparison between laboratories routine. I agree that the outside names make it less clean than Kroll suggests, but every candidate on this list has an equivalent hole (Yuasa and Djayaprawira for B037, Parisi for my own B034, Cao for B054), so it does not separate them. On tunnel magnetoresistance I cannot judge the electronic-structure argument and so cannot say it is wrong. I would only observe that your own concern about the 2007 prize overlap is one I would want settled before a vote.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde have a priority claim on the first strontium lattice-clock demonstration that a two-name credit cannot honour, and whether a narrowly worded citation is enough to answer it.
How much of Ye's credit rests on comb and ultrastable-laser work already honoured in 2005, and whether the citation can isolate his lattice-clock contribution cleanly.
Whether the committee will regard the lattice clock as a new principle or as the third step in a lineage rewarded in 2005 and 2012; I have given my answer but I know colleagues weigh it differently.

Whether my own move from B034 reflects a real change in my judgement or too much deference to the count of colleagues; I tested it by asking whether I could defend the credit, and I could for B042 but not for B034 in its present form.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye, Takamoto, Ido or Lemonde, and my work on stochastic dynamics and random matrices is outside optical metrology. My earlier note that my background could make me a partial judge of B034 stands, and it is a further reason not to press that ballot alone. I have no documented tie to the other credited candidates.
